title: "The 35 BPM Heart: Testing Boris Diaw's Durability Signal in the Box Score"
description: "Can we detect an extraordinary resting heart rate in career statistics? We test E1 (career durability), E3 (shot selection), E2/E4/E5 (within-game resilience) for Boris Diaw against a matched PF cohort using permutation inference."
author: "Kivan Polimis"
date: "2026-10-08"
draft: true
jupyter: blog
categories: [NBA, statistics, sports analytics, durability]
---



## The Claim

In 2016, Boris Diaw reported a resting heart rate of approximately 35 beats per minute — a figure documented in multiple post-retirement interviews and associated with elite endurance athletes, not NBA power forwards. The claim invites a statistical question: if this physiology is real and consequential, can we find its trace in the box score?

We cannot observe heart rate from game logs. But we can ask whether Diaw's durability and late-game performance stand out from a matched cohort of contemporary PFs in ways that are *consistent with* — though not proof of — exceptional cardiovascular capacity.

This post establishes the permutation-inference methodology on Diaw's full career (2004–2016), where BRef play-by-play coverage is complete and no age-regime caveat applies. The [Stockton post](../stockton-durability/index.qmd) applies the same method to a harder case: a longer career, a pre-1996 data gap, and a less-documented physiological claim. The [population study](../nba-durability-population/index.qmd) checks whether either signal holds in the broader BRef-era distribution.

---

## Who to Compare Diaw To

Selection rule: power forwards who debuted 1995–2010, played ≥ 600 career games, averaged ≥ 28 MPG. Six players meet the threshold.

| Player | Career | Active Games | Seasons |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Boris Diaw | 2004–2016 | 1,064 | 14 |
| Dirk Nowitzki | 1998–2019 | 1,522 | 21 |
| Shawn Marion | 1999–2015 | 1,163 | 16 |
| Antawn Jamison | 1999–2014 | 1,083 | 16 |
| Rashard Lewis | 1998–2012 | 777 | 11 |
| Carlos Boozer | 2002–2015 | 861 | 13 |

All players selected on ≥ 600 games — this conditions on the dependent variable for E1. The estimand is durability *among players who completed a long career*, not among all drafted power forwards.

---

## Did He Actually Miss Fewer Games? (E1)

::: {#cell-fig-e1-pf .cell execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Career games missed per 82 — PF cohort. Diaw marked in orange.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e1-pf-output-1.png){#fig-e1-pf fig-alt='Dot plot of games missed per 82-game season for Boris Diaw and 5 PF comparators. Diaw sits at the far left with 4.93 games missed per 82.'}
:::
:::


Diaw missed 4.93 games per 82 over his career — the lowest figure in the reference class, at the 16.7th percentile of the 6-player distribution. The next closest is Dirk Nowitzki at 7.45. The permutation null (5,000 reassignments of the treated label) places the observed gap at p = 0.339, two-sided. With n = 6, the minimum achievable two-sided p is approximately 0.33 — the result is at the floor of what is detectable with this cohort size.

That is a genuine constraint, not a null finding. Diaw sits at the extreme of the distribution; the permutation test cannot reject chance because the reference class is too small to permit it. The gap between Diaw (4.93) and Nowitzki (7.45) is 2.5 games per 82 — sustained over a 14-season career, that gap accumulates to roughly 35 additional games played compared to the next-most-durable player in the cohort. The appropriate inference is that this is *consistent with* an unusual durability advantage, not that the evidence is weak.

**Season correction.** Games-missed-per-82 denominators are adjusted for shortened seasons: 1999 (50 games), 2012 (66 games), 2020 (65 games), 2021 (72 games).

---

## Does Shot Selection Hold Up on Back-to-Back Nights? (E3)

::: {#cell-fig-e3-pf .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Shot selection shift on back-to-back games vs rest — PF cohort. Each point is a player; Diaw labeled.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e3-pf-output-1.png){#fig-e3-pf fig-alt='Scatter of B2B minus rest differences in 3PA/FGA (x-axis) and FTA/FGA (y-axis) for each PF cohort player. Diaw sits in the upper-right corner, showing the largest increase in 3PA/FGA with a moderate FTA/FGA decline.'}
:::
:::


On back-to-back nights, Diaw's three-point attempt rate increases more than any other player in the cohort (Δ = +0.007 per FGA, d = 1.06, 100th percentile). His free-throw attempt rate falls moderately (Δ = −0.033, d = −1.03, 33rd percentile). The shot-selection signature is the inverse of what pure fatigue would predict: a tired player typically avoids the energy cost of running off screens to shoot threes. Diaw instead shifts *toward* lower-contact attempts on consecutive nights — consistent with deliberate load management rather than deterioration, though the same pattern could reflect score margin, opponent scheme, or game script.

For instance, Rashard Lewis shows a similar FTA/FGA decline on B2B (−0.033) but a larger reduction in 3PA/FGA (−0.028) — a pattern more typical of conservative play under fatigue. Diaw's increase in 3PA/FGA is the cohort outlier; the question of whether it reflects a deliberate behavioral adaptation or something structural about his role is not resolvable from game logs alone.

**B2B selection note.** Players in back-to-back games are, by definition, healthy enough to have played the night before. Within-player pairing removes stable effects but not state selection.

---

## Within-Game Resilience: E2, E4, E5

Quarter data is available for four of the six PF cohort players — Diaw, Nowitzki, Marion, and Lewis (the three closest comparators by games-missed-per-82). Boozer and Jamison are not in the within-game window. Unlike the Stockton analysis, there is no age-regime caveat here: Diaw's quarter-level data spans his full BRef career (2004–2016, ages 22–33).

::: {#cell-fig-e2-pf .cell execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![E2: FT% by quarter — Diaw vs PF cohort, 2004–2016. Left: full cohort mean per quarter. Right: Diaw.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e2-pf-output-1.png){#fig-e2-pf fig-alt='Bar charts of mean free throw percentage by quarter for the four-player within-game window. Marion shows the largest Q4 improvement; Diaw declines slightly in Q4.'}
:::
:::


Diaw's Q4 free throw percentage (0.689) is 2.3 percentage points lower than his Q1–Q3 average (0.712) — a slight decline, not resilience. Among the four players in the window, Marion shows the largest Q4 improvement (+4.0 pp, from 0.792 to 0.832), while Nowitzki holds flat (+0.7 pp). Diaw and Lewis both decline slightly (−2.3 and −1.6 pp respectively). The mixed-effects interaction coefficient (Q4 × is_treated) is −0.043 (p = 0.506, two-sided permutation, n = 5,000). With four players in the analysis window, the minimum achievable two-sided p is approximately 0.50 — the result is at the floor of what the test can detect.

The directional finding is clear: Diaw does not show late-game free throw resilience in this window, and Marion — not Diaw — is the Q4 outlier in the favorable direction. This is a genuine null for E2 and should be read as such. The E1 and E3 signals are present; the within-game FT% pattern is not among them. Diaw's durability advantage appears in the aggregate record — fewer missed games, a distinctive B2B shot-selection shift — rather than in within-quarter efficiency.

::: {#cell-fig-e4-pf .cell execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![E4: AST/TOV by quarter — Diaw vs PF cohort. Note: per-quarter AST/TOV is numerically unstable (52% of quarter observations have zero turnovers); this figure is included for completeness but the coefficient estimate is unreliable.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e4-pf-output-1.png){#fig-e4-pf fig-alt='Bar charts of AST/TOV ratio by quarter. The y-axis scale is distorted by zero-turnover quarter-game observations.'}
:::
:::


::: {#cell-fig-e5-pf .cell execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![E5: TS% by quarter — Diaw vs PF cohort. Coverage is too sparse (21% of player-quarter rows non-null) for reliable estimation.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e5-pf-output-1.png){#fig-e5-pf fig-alt='Bar charts of true shooting percentage by quarter. Coverage is sparse because players with no field goal attempts in a quarter contribute no TS% value.'}
:::
:::


E4 (AST/TOV in Q4) and E5 (TS% in Q4) are not interpretable at per-quarter BRef resolution. In 52% of player-quarter observations the turnover count is zero — a normal outcome for any single quarter — which makes the ratio numerically undefined and drives the mixed-effects interaction coefficient to an implausible 42.4. TS% coverage is even thinner: only 21% of player-quarter rows have non-null values, because a player who attempts no field goals in a quarter contributes nothing to the efficiency estimate. Both estimands require coarser aggregation (half-game or full-game) to be usable. This is the same degeneracy observed in the PG cohort — a property of the data resolution, not of these players specifically.

::: {#cell-fig-e6-pf .cell execution_count=7}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![E6: FT% by quarter — PF cohort. Diaw's Q4 free throw percentage (67.7%) is lower than his Q1–Q3 average — a slight decline consistent with the E2 null result. Marion is the Q4 outlier in the favorable direction (82.2%). Nowitzki holds flat across all four quarters.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e6-pf-output-1.png){#fig-e6-pf fig-alt='Line chart of free throw percentage by quarter for Diaw (red) and three PF comparators (gray). Diaw\'s line dips in Q4, while Marion\'s rises and Nowitzki stays flat.'}

### Confounders for within-game estimands

| Confounder | Direction | Mitigation |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Score margin (blowout) | Starters sit; compresses Q4 estimates toward zero | Sensitivity: restricted to games with Q4 margin ≤ 10 |
| Intentional fouling | Inflates FTA in close games; FT% reflects pressure context | FT% (E2) is least-confounded metric |
| Timeout availability | Coaches use Q4 timeouts strategically for recovery | Stated explicitly; not mitigated |

---

## What the Data Can and Cannot Say

**Selection bias.** Cohort conditioned on ≥ 600 career games. E1 describes durability among long-career PFs, a truncated distribution. Interpret percentile ranks accordingly.

**B2B state selection.** Back-to-back comparison is within healthier player-states by construction. Claims are restricted to games actually played.

**Within-game confounders.** Score margin, intentional fouling in close games, and garbage-time rotation changes all affect 4th-quarter statistics in ways BRef box scores do not resolve.

**Causal language.** No result here establishes that Diaw's heart rate *caused* the observed patterns. The findings are *consistent with* the physiology claim and *do not contradict* it. A near-null result is also a legitimate scientific finding — it updates the prior rather than confirming it.

---

## Conclusion

Boris Diaw missed 4.93 games per 82 over 14 seasons — the best figure in a 6-player reference class of matched PF contemporaries, though the permutation p (0.339) sits at the floor of what a n=6 test can detect. The E3 shot-selection result is more distinctive: Diaw is the only player in the cohort who increases his three-point attempt rate on back-to-back nights, a behavioral pattern consistent with deliberate fatigue management — less contact, fewer drives, lower-cost attempts when consecutive-game fatigue is expected — though the causal mechanism is not resolvable from game logs alone.

Within-game, the picture is a genuine null. The four-player quarter-data window (Diaw, Nowitzki, Marion, Lewis) shows Diaw's Q4 free throw percentage declining slightly (−2.3 pp from Q1–Q3 to Q4), while Marion shows the largest improvement (+4.0 pp). The permutation p (0.506) is at the floor for n=4, but the direction is adverse: Diaw is not the Q4 outlier in the favorable direction. E4 (AST/TOV) and E5 (TS%) are not interpretable at per-quarter resolution in either cohort. Unlike the Stockton post, there is no age-regime caveat to invoke here — Diaw's full career is observable, and the null is real.

Diaw's case is the cleaner of the two in this series: full BRef coverage, well-documented sourcing, no age-regime limitation. The durability record (E1) and shot-selection pattern (E3) together constitute a signal worth taking seriously — not proof of the 35 BPM claim, but a box-score record that is harder to explain than random variation. The within-game evidence does not add to that signal, which is itself informative: the advantage, if real, manifests in aggregate availability and conservative shot selection rather than measurable late-quarter efficiency gains.

---
